articles.title: Wiz’s CTO on PHP2Shell and the coming 'vulnpocalypse' | TechCrunch
articles.summary: [jwp-video] The PHP scare may have faded from your feed, but the cleanup is far from over. Last week, two critical bugs in the open source language behind roughly 70% of websites left organizations scrambling to fix their systems, with some taking sites offline until the vulnerabilities could be patched. According to researchers who found the bugs, this is only the beginning, as AI changes how quickly novel vulnerabilities can be uncovered and exploited.   On this episode of TechCrunch’sEquity podcast, Rebecca Bellan talks with Tomer Schwartz, CTO of Exposure Management & AppSec at Google-owned Wiz, who was part of the scramble — alongside OpenAI, research group Calif, and the PHP team — to fix the bugs. On the show, Schwartz and Bellan get into what the race looked like from the inside, how early-stage startups can build with security in mind, and why patching by hand won’t scale.  Subscribe to Equity on YouTube, Apple Podcasts, Overcast, Spotify, and all the casts. You can also follow Equity on X and Threads, at @EquityPod.

On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Rebecca Bellan talks with Tomer Schwartz , CTO of Exposure Management & AppSec at Google-owned Wiz, who was part of the scramble — alongside OpenAI, research group Calif, and the PHP team — to fix the bugs. On the show, Schwartz and Bellan get into what the race looked like from the inside, how early-stage startups can build with security in mind, and why patching by hand won’t scale.

articles.title: The RAM shortage could last years
articles.summary: ﻿Memory makers are only expected to meet 60 percent of demand by the end of 2027.
articles.body: According to Nikkei Asia, even as suppliers ramp up DRAM production, manufacturers are only expected to meet 60 percent of demand by the end of 2027. SK Group chairman has even said that shortages could last until 2030. The world’s largest memory makers — Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron — are all working to add new fabrication capacity, but almost none of it will be online until at least 2027, if not 2028. SK opened a fab in Cheongju in February, but that is the only increase in production among the three for 2026. Nikkei says that production would need to increase by 12 percent a year in 2026 and 2027 to meet demand. But according to Counterpoint Research, an increase of only 7.5 percent is planned. The new facilities will primarily focus on producing high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which is used in AI data centers. With the companies already prioritizing HBM over general-purpose DRAM used in computers and phones, it’s not clear how much these new fabs will help alleviate the price crunch facing consumer electronics. Everything from phones and laptops to VR headsets and gaming handhelds have seen price increases due to the RAM shortage.

articles.title: The New Relationship Minefield: Your Partner’s AI Chats
articles.summary: People are reading their partners' AI chat histories. They can't unsee what they find.
articles.body:
Lindsey Hall's boyfriend was asleep on her shoulder when she accidentally discovered what he'd been telling ChatGPT about her.

Her phone had died, so she picked up his to look up something for work. Then she noticed a chat titled "Relationship Issues and Uncertainty." Inside, she says, were complaints about her appearance, doubts about his attraction to her, and a sentence she still remembers verbatim: "I'm just not proud of her."

While he peacefully snoozed beside her, she learned that ChatGPT had issued a verdict on the state of their relationship: Her boyfriend needed to end it.

When she first saw the chat title, Hall figured it was about a familiar disagreement: She loved her three cats; he wasn't an animal person. "This is probably about the cats," she remembers thinking. She hadn't expected a list of complaints about her. "Nothing was positive," she says. "Not one thing."

Hall got up, collected her toothbrush and charger, and slipped out the front door. "I just had nothing to say," she says. "I had nothing but rage at that point."

Couples have long had ways to discover things they weren't supposed to know about each other: rifling through a journal, stealing a glance at incoming texts, poking around in Instagram or Snapchat DMs. Now, there's another place to look—and plenty to wish you hadn't seen. Therapists say they're working with couples who have discovered their partners asking AI whether they should break up, sharing sexual fantasies, or contemplating how to bring up something they were too nervous to say out loud.

Why a partner's AI chats can feel like a betrayal

Reading the chats doesn't necessarily tell you what the other person meant. Was your partner venting after a fight or seriously considering leaving you? Were they asking for help talking to you—or finding a way to avoid it? And who owes whom an apology : the person who read the chats, or the one who shared intimate details about their partner with a chatbot?

When Ilana Grines, a licensed marriage and family therapist in Los Angeles, works with couples, her first question is now: "What have you told AI?" She wants to know if and how both people are using it, what they're sharing, and whether they've discussed any of that with each other. Most haven't, she says.

"We don't have a language around our conversations with AI," Grines says. Couples may understand that a journal is private without having discussed whether the same goes for a chatbot conversation. When someone discovers their partner's chats, "it creates this huge rupture where one person accessed the other person's history," Grines says. "And then it's nuclear."

One couple Grines worked with paid for a single AI subscription. The wife, a teacher, used it to grade papers. Her husband used it to explore sexual fantasies, apparently without realizing that conversations from his computer would be visible through their shared account, Grines says. His wife discovered the topic in the platform's sidebar.

"We know about a third person entering our relationship," Grines says. "But we don't know about this third space that we're creating."

Sometimes, one partner doesn't even know that space exists. They might be aware their partner asks AI for help with work or vacation planning—not that they're also discussing their sex life or wondering whether to stay together. Hall used chatbots herself, but discussing her relationship with one hadn't occurred to her. "I just didn't think of it as a tool for that," she says.

Part of what stings is realizing your partner talked to a chatbot about something they felt like they couldn't bring up with you, says Shemiah Derrick, a relationship therapist in Chicago. You might also wonder how long they've been feeling this way—and whether you would have known if you hadn't read the chats.

Derrick has seen couples finally talk through a problem—only to start fighting when one person admits they used AI to figure out what to say. The other person's reaction, as she describes it: "You had to go to chat for us to do that?"

In those cases, Derrick points out that the person turned to AI because their usual way of bringing up problems wasn't working. They wanted to get through a tough conversation without having the same old fight. "They were trying to do something different," she says.

What AI chats can reveal about relationships

Giulia P. Davis, a licensed marriage and family therapist in San Francisco, recalls working with a couple after one partner read the other's AI chats without permission and found complaints and doubts about their relationship. The person who wrote them was still sorting out how they felt. Their partner assumed they'd already made up their mind.

"The partner didn't find a straightforward confession or plan to leave the relationship," Davis says.

Davis helped them distinguish "what you really think" from "what you might think about." Someone might complain to a chatbot after a fight or ask what would happen if they broke up, for example, but not feel that way once they've cooled down.

If you find these types of messages, you should ask your partner how they're feeling, Davis suggests—not assume everything they typed is something they've been hiding from you. "A person can have private thoughts without being deceptive," she says. "Couples need boundaries around private digital spaces just as they do around journals, therapy, or conversations with trusted friends."

A chatbot also does something a journal doesn't: It answers. But remember that it's getting only one side of the story, says Shayce Johnston, a licensed mental health counselor in Gainesville, Fla., and the founder of Human AI Dynamics, which explores how people form emotional and relational bonds with AI. If your partner complains about you and the chatbot agrees, they may feel that someone else has confirmed you're in the wrong. Johnston describes the reaction this way: "Even the AI agrees with me." That doesn't make it true.

How to set boundaries around AI in a relationship

Don't assume you and your partner agree on what should stay private, says Tammy Nelson, a psychotherapist in Los Angeles and author of Open Monogamy: A Guide to Co-Creating Your Ideal Relationship Agreement . You might think nothing of opening their ChatGPT account; they might consider it the equivalent of reading their journal. Talk about that before you're staring at something you wish you hadn't seen.

"What parts are private?" Nelson asks. Keeping a password to yourself, for example, doesn't automatically mean you're concealing something that would hurt your partner. "I really do think that it's important to revisit that conversation pretty often," she says.

Reading the chats is only part of the issue. What's OK to put into them? Johnston works with couples in which one person uses AI enthusiastically while the other has privacy, ethical, or environmental concerns. Your partner might be fine with you asking for date-night ideas but uncomfortable with you pasting in their texts or describing your sex life.

Grines suggests starting with a question: "Can you share something you've asked AI about our relationship?" You can also ask whether there are subjects they find easier to discuss with a chatbot than with you. The answers can help you get specific about what you're both comfortable with: using AI to prepare for a difficult conversation, for example, or talking through an argument afterward. Discuss whether those exchanges will stay private or whether you'd like to share what came out of them.

If you're tempted to skip the conversation and start scrolling through your partner's chat history, Nelson suggests asking yourself why. Has something happened that makes you distrust them, or are you feeling anxious and hoping what you find will reassure you?

As Davis puts it: "What gets in the way of asking your partner directly?"

What to do after reading your partner's AI chats

If you've read something upsetting, ask your partner what it meant before assuming you know. Davis encourages couples to wait until they're calm enough to have that conversation. The person who used AI can explain what they were working through; the person who read the chats can explain what hurt.

Johnston wants couples to stop treating the chat history as a verdict on their relationship. Instead, she helps them understand "what the need was, what the fear is, and where the disconnection was that led to the conversation in the first place." That means making room for both people's feelings: You can be hurt by what your partner wrote, and they can be upset that you read it without permission.

There may still be a useful role for AI in the relationship. Grines has worked with couples who use their therapy notes to ask a chatbot for questions they can discuss together at home, for example. Johnston sometimes encourages clients to rehearse a difficult conversation with AI before having it with their partner.

"I don't think AI is inherently anti-relationship," Grines says. But she wants couples to consider whether it's helping them talk to each other—or becoming the only place they're willing to be honest. "AI can be a bridge into communication," she says, "or it can be a place where communication goes to die."

For Hall, finding out how her boyfriend used AI made her question conversations she'd once felt good about. Before meeting in person, they'd spent months messaging. He'd seemed warm over text, she says, but could be colder face-to-face. She'd wondered: "What am I doing wrong?"

His chat history offered a possible explanation. When they'd discussed serious or emotional subjects, she says, he'd pasted her messages into ChatGPT and asked it to help him respond. She remembers his instruction: "Placate her."

She still wonders whether he would have spoken so harshly about her to another person, or whether something about talking to AI encouraged him. "Would you have said all those things to a person in that way?" she asks.

After she left his house, he began texting her. She turned off her phone. When he later came to her home, she told him she'd read the chats. By then, she says, she felt there was little left to discuss: "I just read exactly how you feel."

articles.title: Voters in Texas agree: They hate data centers
articles.summary: Fury over data centers has become a major issue for voters in Texas and could influence key midterm election races.
articles.body: Ask Texas NAACP president Gary Bledsoe what it’s been like to see data center developers descend upon Austin and its surrounding suburbs and he can rattle off project after project facing opposition from locals. There’s the fight in Taylor over plans to build a data center at a site that’s supposed to be a park. Temple, around 40 miles away, is another sore spot, Bledsoe says. The mayor and City Council members there face recall attempts over data center developments. And some 30 miles outside of Austin, San Marcos became the first city in all of Texas to ban data centers. Nowhere in the world are data centers growing more explosively than in Texas. With the midterm elections looming, the data center fight “is the issue in Texas,” says Bledsoe. The state’s NAACP recently joined dozens of other groups across the political spectrum to form a coalition to stop — or at least stall — data center construction. Their grievances are just as diverse as their membership: concerns about how much water the industry consumes in a state as dry as Texas, qualms about tax subsidies, and objections to new gas plants and wind farms built to meet rising electricity demand. Together, Bledsoe estimates the coalition — named We the People Texas — represents as many as 1 million voters across the state. If there’s one thing a broad range of voters can agree on this election season, it’s that they hate data centers and are unhappy with the status quo. A majority of Texans — 57 percent — oppose the construction of data centers, an August poll found. That included 43 percent of Republicans, 75 percent of Democrats, and 54 percent of independents. After initially proclaiming his state the “epicenter of AI development,” Texas Gov. Greg Abbott is now fighting for reelection against underdog Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who is seen as having a rare shot at taking a reliably red state. The state’s high-profile Senate race is no less of a nail-biter, with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton running neck and neck against Democrat James Talarico. In each race, candidates have to win over voters who think data centers are coming for their water, land, and livelihoods. Republican and Democratic hopefuls alike are trying to distance themselves from an industry that’s taken deep root in the state — and so far, voters aren’t buying it. “You’re talking about Democrats, libertarians, independents, Republicans, all in one fight … we have almost nothing in common in so many other ways. And yet you get us in the room with this issue, and it’s like a wall … fighting one big enemy,” says Jet Parker, who cofounded a group called Save Rural Texas that is now part of the We the People Texas coalition. Save Rural Texas came together this year after a local county commissioners’ meeting about plans to build a new data center in the Texoma area that borders Oklahoma. Residents, including Parker, successfully delayed that project. That victory led Parker, a corporate coach and speaker, to write up a handbook for other communities trying to block data center projects, and she now spends much of her time traveling around the state to train grassroots groups. She’s got a warning for Republicans: If they keep backing data centers, they’ll lose Texas. “You just pissed off a lot of people in rural Texas who are supposed to carry you across the [finish] line,” Parker says. Abbott is in particularly hot water. “You brung it, so you dance with it. That’s Texas talk, you know,” Parker says. “That’s what Abbott’s done, but we’re the ones having to dance with it … we didn’t want to be in the dance at all.” For years, however, Texas has taken among the most welcoming stances toward data centers in the country. The state passed a sales and use tax exemption for data centers in 2013 under former Gov. Rick Perry. In 2015, Abbott expanded the exemption to include hyperscale data centers, which can span millions of square feet and house tens of thousands of GPUs. As a result, qualifying data center developers don’t have to pay state taxes on equipment and electricity for up to 20 years. That essentially rolled out the red carpet for companies that need abundant electricity to power energy-hungry data centers. Since then data centers have had a massive growth spurt in order to support new generative AI models — and that’s costing the state. The tax exemption was initially expected to cost taxpayers $14.6 million in 2014 and 2015. But in 2025, state officials estimated that the tax break would lead to $3.2 billion in lost sales tax revenue over two years. The state’s energy woes go further than that. Electricity bills have grown by 35.4 percent on average over the past five years as demand rises and utilities build expensive new infrastructure to meet that demand. Bledsoe is concerned about air pollution for communities around new gas plants. Data center electricity demand could erase decades of air quality gains in Texas, one recent study found. Parker, meanwhile, can’t stand solar and wind farms built near farmland. Neither wants to see new transmission lines snaking through their communities. Data centers can also put pressure on already stressed water supplies, especially in a drought-prone state like Texas. While they can reuse water used on-site to cool servers, the larger part of data centers’ water footprint comes from electricity use. Data center proposals have driven a surge of gas and nuclear power projects, both of which need a lot of water for their own cooling systems. Data center electricity demand could increase nearly tenfold by 2030, the state’s largest grid operator estimates. Meanwhile, data centers in Texas consumed about 25 billion gallons of water last year, around 0.4 percent of total water use, according to the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). By 2030, that figure could grow to up to 2.7 percent of the state’s total annual water use, HARC estimates. And water consumption can be much higher when zooming into certain communities. Another study by the University of Texas at Austin estimated that data center water use statewide could rise to as high as 9 percent by 2040. Virginia has historically been the state with the most data centers, but it’s running out of space. Virginia still beats Texas 287 to 170 when it comes to the number of planned data center projects as of April, according to Pew Research. But as data centers get bigger, they’re moving out of cities and into rural areas — particularly in Texas. Data center capacity is typically measured by how much power it draws, and in this measure, Texas already takes the crown with 26GW of existing and under-construction capacity compared to 13GW in Virginia. Facing backlash to data centers, Abbott has changed his tune. In June, he directed the state Public Utility Commission to require that data center operators cover the costs of new infrastructure built to serve them. Since then, he has also announced statewide moratoriums on permits for data center projects pending audits on their electricity and water use. He’s also said that he would support a repeal of the sales tax exemption for data centers and greater oversight of data centers’ water and electricity use. Even so, he’s reportedly taken millions in campaign contributions from data center interests, and We the People Texas coalition members are not convinced he’s turned the page. “Is he doing enough? Absolutely not,” Parker says. The NAACP sent a letter to Abbott’s office last month criticizing his moratoriums for not going far enough because the state is only auditing projects that connect to the power grid. However, more so than any other state, Texas has data centers building their own power supply on-site, without needing to connect to the grid. Bledsoe’s concerned that these private energy projects will be subject to less regulatory scrutiny, while also harming air quality in nearby neighborhoods. Projects that already have permits are still being built. And an October investigation by advocacy group Public Citizen and FracTracker found public records indicating that state agencies are still processing permits for data centers, although Abbott’s office denies that they have issued any approvals since he directed them to pause permitting. To Bledsoe and other coalition members, he says, the temporary moratorium looks like “an attempt to run out the clock before the election.” Data center hyperscalers including AWS, Microsoft, Google, Meta, and others have formed their own trade group called the Data Center Coalition (DCC). For what it’s worth, DCC isn’t endorsing any candidates. But in an interview with The Verge, Jess Heck, the group’s director of Texas government affairs, says, “It’s very clear that our members share the same goals as Gov. Abbott and the legislature. We want to be true partners, good neighbors in every Texas community where we operate.” Heck didn’t confirm whether any of its members are providing any campaign support for Abbott. Eduardo Leal, press secretary for Abbott’s campaign, said in an email to The Verge that “Under [Abbott’s] standards, data centers must pay for their own electric infrastructure, add power instead of only adding demand, reuse their own water, reduce the cost of electricity for Texans, not disrupt residential neighborhoods, and eliminate reliance on outdated taxpayer-funded incentives.” Abbott signed a state Senate bill into law last year that directs the Public Utility Commission of Texas to reassess how it allocates transmission costs in order to keep rates from rising disproportionately for residential customers. And this June, he proposed more measures to force companies to cover the costs of infrastructure upgrades needed to serve their data centers. Abbott’s biggest competitor, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, has eked out a narrow lead recently in some polls after strengthening her language against data centers — calling for a moratorium on development until the state legislature passes more protections. “I think her campaign has made a ton of inroads into moderate Republican communities because of her stance on data centers,” says Anthony Elmo, public education funding defender for Good Jobs First, which recently cofounded another coalition pushing for data center reforms in Texas alongside other advocacy groups. Hinojosa has skyrocketed from a relatively obscure local official to a serious contender for the governor’s seat, largely on a populist message that caters to residents’ frustration with Big Tech companies grabbing land for data centers. Even so, she might not be convincing enough for conservative rural voters. Candidates from both sides of the aisle were pretty soft on data centers up until the party conventions earlier this year, says Miriam Cobb, who cofounded the Texas Coalition Against Data Centers earlier this year (which is also part of We the People Texas). Texans can see the political posturing from Hinojosa, too, she says. One of Hinojosa’s major donors has been the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, which recently formed an “American Infrastructure Alliance” with OpenAI and data center developers. “[Voters] know she wasn’t against it from a place of understanding or sincerity, it’s something she knows she has to say now,” Cobb tells The Verge, adding that she’ll be writing in an independent candidate come Election Day. Even with many conservatives — some of them now claiming to be single-issue voters on data centers — skeptical of both parties’ candidates, Cobb still expects Republicans to lose seats. Paxton, the Republican candidate for Senate, is attempting to atone for his previous support of data centers. He voted for the sales tax exemptions as a state senator in 2013, although he now says he’d support a repeal. In September, he announced an investigation into hundreds of data centers’ water use. Paxton also launched an investigation into the case in Taylor over whether it’s legal for land deeded for parkland to be developed into a data center. And he’s aligned himself with Abbott’s proposals to impose stronger light and noise restrictions on data centers, limit construction in rural areas, and push developers to cover the costs of new energy infrastructure. But he also reportedly received hundreds of thousands of dollars in campaign funding this year from data center interests. Talarico, meanwhile, has a similar plan to stop data centers “from jacking up our utility bills.” But he also claims to want to “empower local communities to decide whether they want a data center in their town,” a jab at Republicans including Paxton who have either stayed mum on whether counties should be allowed to make permitting decisions on data centers rather than the state or have actively curtailed their ability to do so. Abbott signed the so-called “Death Star” bill into law in 2023 barring counties and municipalities from crafting regulations that contradict state law. Some Republicans have cited the Death Star law in legal challenges to local moratoriums on data centers. While the Senate race between Talarico and Paxton is in the national spotlight over the prospect of a Democrat flipping the seat, it’s probably less important for Texans concerned most about data centers, advocates tell The Verge. The race is too politically polarized to flip voters on the single issue, Cobb says, and neither candidate has given a very convincing position on how to rein in data centers anyway. Neither campaign responded to press inquiries from The Verge. Working at the federal level, the best thing the senator-elect could do would be to push back against President Donald Trump’s data center agenda and ensure Texas can moderate data center development without interference, she says. “We want assurances that you’re gonna let us deal with it instead of what’s been happening, where Trump keeps saying, you know, ‘Let them in, let them in, let them in,’” Cobb tells The Verge. Cobb still sees construction traffic clogging two-lane rural roads leading to data center projects that have avoided Abbott’s partial moratorium. Residents are worried about the traffic jams blocking emergency vehicles, especially when fire weather kicks up. In some areas, Texans have seen property values drop, she adds. Farmers are giving up land that their families have tended to for generations. In other neighborhoods, an influx of new workers arriving for the data center “gold rush” is exacerbating housing shortages and making rent more unaffordable for locals. In either case, data center opposition coalition members say they’re worried about a loss of culture. “It’s not for nothing,” Cobb says. “They have real community … and now they’re losing it.”

articles.title: Anthropic’s Tensions With Trump Laid Bare Ahead of Landmark IPO
articles.summary: Anthropic PBC is cautioning investors that its outspoken advocacy for artificial intelligence safety could make the company the target of government retaliat...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Anthropic PBC is cautioning investors that its outspoken advocacy for artificial intelligence safety could make the company the target of government retaliation, highlighting the unusual degree of government-related risk to its future business after a year of skirmishes with the Trump administration.

Ahead of its landmark initial public offering, Anthropic said in a filing that its positions on AI oversight and the views expressed by its executives could expose it to significant levels of government pressure, alluding to the company's feuds with Trump officials over how to safely develop the technology.

"We have experienced, and may continue to experience, increased visibility and may continue to be subject to heightened scrutiny or the risk of being disproportionately or selectively targeted by particular governmental bodies, even where similarly situated companies are not," Anthropic said in a prospectus setting the stage for its expected public listing next month.

The comments, buried deep in Monday's filing, pointed to tensions with the administration that took root in a dispute early this year over guardrails on Pentagon use of the firm's technology. More recently, Anthropic has clashed with officials over whether its cutting-edge Mythos model was safe enough for public release, and its Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei continues to run afoul of President Donald Trump with his support for a coordinated AI slowdown to give safety teams time to catch up with the technology.

Investors must now decide how to weigh the regulatory risks facing a firm whose technology is accessible enough to be pitched as a product for daily consumer use yet powerful enough to be considered a cyber weapon and a potential catalyst of biological warfare that warrants closer scrutiny. For Anthropic, that history of dust-ups with the administration adds to the uncertainty looming over the entire AI industry.

"With AI, the boundaries of government authority are still being ironed out, sometimes through direct confrontations with individual companies," said Sarah Kreps, director of the Tech Policy Institute at Cornell University. "It's hard for investors to price in that kind of uncertainty."

articles.title: xAI is buying out homeowners who promise not to sue over data center noise
articles.summary: Elon Musk’s xAI has offered to buy homes in the Southaven, Mississippi neighborhood, as long as they don’t join a lawsuit targeting its nearby data center and power plant.
articles.body: A subsidiary of Elon Musk’s xAI is offering to buy up homes in a Mississippi neighborhood, as long as residents don’t join a lawsuit targeting the company’s nearby data center and power plant, according to a report from The Guardian. A realtor going door-to-door in the Southaven neighborhood reportedly told one resident that xAI plans to purchase 418 homes, adding that 18 homeowners already have plans to sell. People who rent homes in the area report they’re already being forced out, with 60 days’ notice after their landlords agreed to sell. A recent report from the Mississippi Free Press includes a letter received by several households recently, reading in part: > MZX denies all of the allegations against it. However, because MZX also requires property for its business purposes, MZX, through its real estate broker, is offering to purchase real estate in Southaven in exchange for, among other things, a release of all claims related to the lawsuit. If you decide to accept MZX’s offer, MZX will ask you to sign a real estate contract under which you will agree to execute a separate release agreement at the closing of the real estate transaction. > Importantly, by executing the Release Agreement, you will be releasing possible claims you might have related to the Southaven Plant, including any claims you may have in connection with the Haley action. After executing the Release Agreement, you will be unable to recover any damages or other relief from the Haley lawsuit, and you will also be unable to bring claims on your own behalf. The Release Agreement provides further details on which claims would be released. As reported by The Guardian, xAI offered to purchase the homes if the owners don’t join a lawsuit filed by three residents, who accuse the company’s massive data center and gas-fired turbines of emitting “near-constant noise” and vibrations. xAI has ramped up its data center buildout over the past couple of years, constructing two sprawling “Colossus” facilities in Memphis, while bringing its “Macrohardrr” data center and an accompanying power plant to Southaven, which is located just over the Tennessee border. Growing opposition to AI data centers is putting pressure on politicians in the weeks leading up to the midterm elections. Last week, Memphis City Council voted down a one-year moratorium on AI data center development, and instead adopted an ordinance that would pause construction for 135 days. After Mississippi’s governor touted the company’s plan to invest more than $20 billion in the area earlier this year, SpaceXAI recently reported it’s facing up to $6.1 million in potential civil penalties for environmental law violations, along with more than $220 million in claims of unpaid bills for work performed at the Memphis and Southaven sites. In addition to a lawsuit filed by residents, xAI is also facing legal action from the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP), which accuses the company of operating dozens of unpermitted methane gas turbines in Southaven. A federal judge blocked the Trump administration’s attempt to dismiss the lawsuit earlier this month.

articles.title: Chrome’s enhanced autofill can now pull info from Gmail to help you fill out forms
articles.summary: Google is improving Chrome’s enhanced autofill capabilities in the US today by adding users’ Gmail accounts as another source of info.
articles.body: Following improvements made to Chrome’s enhanced autofill last year that included your name, passport number, email address, and physical addresses sourced from your Google Accounts and services like Google Wallet, the feature is now expanding. Starting today, Chrome’s enhanced autofill will use Gemini with Personal Intelligence to suggest information sourced from your Gmail, potentially saving you from having to search for confirmation emails, receipts, or shipping updates yourself. The expanded autofill capabilities can retrieve details such as a shipment’s tracking number, travel details like a flight booking number or hotel reservation, or the order number of a recent purchase. Sensitive data presented as a suggestion while completing a form remains encrypted, and users can manage what enhanced autofill has access to in Chrome’s settings, or turn it off completely. [Image: Chrome can suggest details automatically pulled from your Gmail account so you can complete forms without constantly hopping between browser tabs. Google is starting to roll out the enhanced autofill improvements today in the US. They’ll be available through Gemini in Chrome for users with Personal Intelligence turned on in the desktop, Android, and iOS versions of the browser.

articles.title: Anthropic just launched tools to show companies what their AI spending is buying | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The frontier lab is lifting the curtain on how users spend money on its models ahead of a planned IPO.
articles.body:
The financials Anthropic shared with investors this week suggest that its AI coding tool, Claude Code, is every bit the business success the frontier lab wanted. The company recorded an operating profit in the second quarter, and 900% net revenue retention — that is, spending from the same customers in Q3 2025 grew nine times in Q3 2026.

Anthropic has focused on getting enterprise users to stick around and Wednesday announced a new suite of reporting tools designed to give those customers a more granular understanding of the value they get from their token spend.

Using internal analytics and employee surveys, managers can view a team’s work over a given date range, what the team produced, how much it cost, and where its workflows broke down. Anthropic says it won’t use this data for model training by default. The reports will also offer recommendations on how to improve the results.

This is a clear attempt to demonstrate the return on investment of Anthropic’s tools and to show customers how to improve it — a major concern among large customers. Anthropic is also creating pooled group budgets to allow teams to better manage token spending.

Businesses have been hunting for that kind of information as they figure out how best to deploy AI tools. While usage among venture-backed firms is driving token spend, most of the Fortune 500 are not seeing major gains from deploying AI.

Jellyfish, a company that makes tools for software developers, released a new report yesterday based on the use of agentic coding tools by 276,000 of its customers. Claude Code and other tools built on Anthropic models remain the most widely used in the survey, responsible for nearly a third of all proposed code changes submitted for review. More importantly, spending on those tools has grown 10x since the beginning of the year, with their cost now equal to about 2% of total engineering cost.

“Even if you’re saying 2% is still small, that 10x growth is growth that most CFOs didn’t plan for,” Nicholas Arcolano, the chief scientist at Jellyfish, told TechCrunch. We’re certainly getting to the point where people are realizing, okay, it’s not enough to just spend a bunch. You now have to optimize it, make it work.”

Anthropic’s new reports speak to that challenge. Anthropic leads among enterprise customers, but what makes an agentic coding tool truly sticky is difficult to identify. The release of OpenAI’s Astra model this summer seemed like a potential threat to Anthropic, but so far it hasn’t slowed Anthropic’s adoption numbers.

“It took a long time for us to see Codex really pop in our data at all, and it has come up with Astra [OpenAI’s latest model],” Nikolas Albarran, the AI product lead at Jellyfish, told TechCrunch. Looking at X, he continued, you’d get the distinct impression that the competition is more heated. “Everyone in the Valley is like, ‘Oh, Codex is better.’” In reality, Albarran continued, “Anthropic was just there with great enterprise motions, and they had an incumbent weight of their own — this stuff just worked and worked well, and a lot of people just put a lot of effort into standardizing workflows around it. And there’s not a big enough reason to switch.”

It’s not just a question of models and workflows, either. The realities of business mean that once a frontier lab has gotten its hooks into a customer, switching is harder than it is compared to an individual programmer or small organization. Albarran points to the investment all the major AI labs are making in forward-deployed engineering (FDE) organizations, teams that embed AI consultants inside customer organizations to help them get off the ground. These new reporting tools can be seen as a kind of FDE-lite, a lighter version of that hands-on help, for Anthropic customers.

“We’re at a point now where it’s mature enough, where once you’re in, it’s going to be harder and harder to switch because you’ve spent the effort,” he said. “Even if they’re all mostly the same, they’re all going to be slightly different, have their own slight quirks of how they handle agent.md files, etc., and so that cost to switch is not zero.”

articles.title: DOJ Inquires About Nvidia’s Hugging Face Deal, Reuters Says
articles.summary: The US Justice Department is making inquiries about Nvidia Corp.’s agreement to acquire AI model company Hugging Face for about $13 billion, part of broader...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The US Justice Department is making inquiries about Nvidia Corp.'s agreement to acquire AI model company Hugging Face for about $13 billion, part of broader regulatory scrutiny of the chip giant, Reuters reported.

The department is exploring how the transaction may affect competition in the artificial intelligence market, the news agency said, citing unidentified people familiar with the situation. At the same time, the DOJ is continuing a yearslong probe into the chipmaker's conduct, Reuters said.

Nvidia announced the Hugging Face deal in September, touting the purchase as a way to protect the open-source software community. Developers rely on the Hugging Face platform to share models and data that can be freely used by anyone. As part of the deal, Nvidia has vowed to keep the platform open.

The Justice Department has inquired whether the acquisition will let Nvidia control a key distribution point for AI, according to Reuters.

A representative for Nvidia declined to comment. Hugging Face didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Justice Department said it doesn't typically comment on matters before it under longstanding policy. "We can affirm that this DOJ under President Trump's leadership will continue to prioritize advancement of Super Intelligence for the betterment of the American people," the department said in a statement, using the administration's preferred term for AI.

Nvidia, the world's most valuable company, has parlayed its dominance in AI chips into a role in other markets, including software, AI models and networking equipment.

Bloomberg News reported last month that the DOJ was investigating whether Nvidia structured a $20 billion licensing agreement with AI chip startup Groq Inc. to avoid antitrust review. Though Groq remained an independent company after that deal, the startup's chief executive officer and operating chief moved to Nvidia as part of the transaction. Some US lawmakers later said the agreement was a takeover that stifled competition.

More recently, Nvidia has been discussing a deal with startup Reflection AI, Bloomberg has reported. That startup, which is already backed by Nvidia, debuted an open-weight model earlier this month. With such software, developers release the model's parameters, or weights, allowing others to freely use and modify the technology.

articles.title: Google launches Gemini 4 Carbon with a ‘significant leap’ in cybersecurity
articles.summary: Google has launched Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier model that the company says offers “significant gains” in coding, agentic tasks, and cybersecurity.
articles.body: Google has released its latest frontier model, Gemini 4 Carbon, offering “significant gains” in coding, agentic tasks, and cybersecurity. In an announcement on Wednesday, Google highlights Carbon’s top spot on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (v5.0) benchmark, with Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra trailing behind. The new Gemini 4 Carbon model offers improvements over Argon, which Google released earlier this month. It’s currently only available to a select group of cybersecurity defense companies, but it will eventually expand to other partners in its Fairwind Program. [Image: Carbon sits ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. The company says Carbon reflects the “pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward,” coming with a “significant leap” in cyberdefense that makes it better at finding vulnerabilities and generating secure code. Carbon currently holds the number one spot on SEC-bench Pro, a benchmark that measures an AI model’s ability to discover real-world bugs, and ExploitGym, which measures how a model can turn a vulnerability into exploits. [Image: Gemini 4 Carbon also beat GPT-6 Astra on the SEC-bench Pro cybersecurity benchmark. Google says Gemini 4 Carbon is built for completing longer tasks, adding that its internal teams have seen it “run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks.” It’s also better at avoiding shortcuts, resisting prompt injection attacks, and collaborating with users, according to Google. Carbon is supposed to offer more “transparency and honesty” as well, by cutting “unsupported claims” by two times when compared to Argon. It will launch at the same competitive introductory price as Argon, at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.

articles.title: Microsoft recorded $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Microsoft said it made $10 billion in revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments, in the quarter ending September 30. It underscores the still-enormous financial dependency of the partnership.
articles.body:
Microsoft generated $10 billion in revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments, in the quarter ended September 30, the company said in a regulatory filing on Wednesday. That represents nearly 11% of Microsoft’s total quarterly revenue of $92.3 billion, highlighting the enormous financial ties that remain between the two companies even as they increasingly compete for the same customers .

(Microsoft’s financial year begins in July, making the quarter ended September 30, 2026 the first quarter of its fiscal 2027.)

For the full 2026 fiscal year, revenue from OpenAI hit $24.1 billion. At its latest quarterly pace, Microsoft would pull in $40 billion annually from OpenAI-related arrangements.

Microsoft also reported $7.2 billion in outstanding receivables from OpenAI at the end of September, up from $6 billion at the end of June. That money represents amounts OpenAI owes for previous transactions, not additional revenue.

It’s not clear how much of Microsoft’s revenue from OpenAI came from revenue-sharing payments or Azure cloud computing services. TechCrunch has reached out for more information. In November 2025, TechCrunch reported , citing leaked documents, that Microsoft had received $865.8 million in net revenue-sharing payments from OpenAI during the first nine months of that year.

OpenAI reportedly shares 20% of its revenue with Microsoft as part of a previous deal in which the software giant invested more than $13 billion in the AI startup. (Neither the AI lab nor Microsoft have publicly confirmed this percentage.) As part of an April 2026 agreement, OpenAI is on the hook to continue sharing revenue with Microsoft through 2030, subject to a cap, even as OpenAI is allowed to work with competing cloud providers.

The companies began loosening the ties of their once-exclusive partnership in October 2025, when Microsoft relinquished its hold on OpenAI to give the startup more freedom to partner with other cloud providers. In exchange, OpenAI committed to buying an additional $250 billion in Azure services as part of an October 2025 agreement.

Microsoft’s ownership stake in OpenAI has also declined slightly from about 25% in June to 24% in September. That continues a gradual decline from roughly 27% following the October 2025 recapitalization. Microsoft did not specify what caused the dilution.

articles.title: Google expands AI Search ads globally as core ad growth slows
articles.summary: The announcement came alongside parent company Alphabet's third-quarter earnings report, which saw revenue grow 25% year over year to $127.6 billion.
articles.body:
Google is bringing ads in its AI-powered Search experiences to international markets, betting that generative AI can open up new revenue opportunities even as growth in its core search advertising business slows.

The announcement came Wednesday during Alphabet's third-quarter earnings call, as the company reported $127.6 billion in revenue, up 25% year over year. But Search advertising growth continued to decelerate, and Alphabet shares fell 8% following the results.

Google Search revenue grew 12% year over year in the third quarter, down from 17% growth in the second quarter and 19% in the first quarter. The slowdown puts added pressure on Google to turn its expanding AI features into a meaningful source of advertising revenue.

"We are now scaling high-quality ads within AI overviews in AI mode to more users and queries," Philipp Schindler, Google's chief business officer, said during the call with investors. "This includes taking our monetization footprint global for the first time. Today, we're announcing the expansion of ads in AI mode into international markets alongside multi-turn ads and AI mode in the U.S."

Google says early results suggest the formats are working. Click-through rates for sponsored product listings in AI Mode are already comparable to those for organic listings, according to Schindler. The company's user research also indicates that people find the ads relevant.

The move builds on Google's May announcement of new Gemini-powered ad formats, including conversational discovery ads that respond to users' questions and sponsored recommendations integrated into AI-generated answers.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai also said that Search queries grew at their fastest year-over-year rate in five years, though he did not disclose the exact growth rate. He credited AI features with changing how people use Search, including prompting longer and more complex queries.

Queries in AI Mode are three times longer on average than traditional searches, Pichai said, while one in five AI Mode searches globally involves voice, images, or documents. Google has also surpassed 50 billion visual searches per month.

"[Search] is bringing the benefits of AI to more people than any other product in the world," Pichai told investors. "People are using our AI features more, searching in entirely new ways. Their queries are longer, personalized, and multimodal."

Alphabet's Google Services division, which includes Search, generated $96.3 billion in revenue, up 11% year over year. Google Cloud revenue surged 103% to $30.7 billion.

The results follow a busy quarter for Google, including the release of Gemini 4 Argon , the growth of the Gemini app to 1 billion monthly users , and the launch of its Pixel 11 lineup .

articles.title: AI used to remove visible differences from photographs criticised
articles.summary: An AI tool edited a photo of Rhiannon Morgan in a work newsletter and she was shocked by the results.
articles.body:
People with scars, birthmarks and medical conditions have told the BBC how AI tools have changed or erased their personal features.

Rhiannon Morgan, from Bridgend, said an image of her used in a work newsletter had been auto-retouched by AI.

A BBC Wales investigation found AI tools including Elon Musk's Grok, Google's Gemini and OpenAI's ChatGPT removed visible differences when prompted to make a person look "normal".

AI did not make any other changes to the person's clothing, hair or to people in the background.

The charity Changing Faces estimates there are about five million people in the UK affected by a visible difference including skin conditions or characteristics that set an individual apart from the conventional societal norm.

It said it was unacceptable that people were excluded from AI or are made to conform to narrow beauty standards.

"When I'm out in public I expect stares or comments but when it comes to you in your workplace or at home it feels a bit more personal," Rhiannon, 30, said.

She has a rare genetic condition called epidermolytic ichthyosis which means her skin grows too fast.

This makes it prone to blistering and causes her significant mobility issues.

She understands the software programme Canva was asked to re-arrange the photos in the work newsletter, not to edit them.

But the final result shocked Rhiannon, and she said: "It was one of those really jarring moments where I thought I don't know who that person is."

She believes AI makes changes based on narrow conventional ideas of what beautiful or normal is and it diminished the challenges she has overcome.

"In the picture I was speaking, so my hands were up. I'm quite pink usually and that had gone," she said.

"I've also got hard skin on my hands and that had also been smoothed over."

Luckily, Rhiannon saw the image before it was sent out.

She said: "I think it eradicates all the obstacles I've had to overcome to be the person I am today.

"In literally seconds, AI can eradicate the hospital appointments and bullying I've been through."

Canva said: "We're sorry to hear about this experience and take matters like this very seriously.

"Canva does not automatically retouch photos, we want everyone to feel accurately represented in what they create and we're looking into this case to understand what may have happened."

This issue was raised by campaigner Katie Piper after someone uploaded a photo of her and asked Grok to "fix her face", prompting her to question what right does AI have to define what is "normal"?

In July, the TV presenter posted on social media, saying: "So, today I found out what I'd look like if I was 'normal'… according to AI and thousands of strangers on the internet.

"Someone uploaded a photo of me to Grok and asked it to 'fix her face'."

The former model has had hundreds of surgeries to repair damage to her face and eyesight following an attack in 2008 on the orders of her ex-boyfriend when she was 24.

Her post gained thousands of supportive comments and she posed the question: "What happens when AI decides what 'normal' looks like?"

BBC Wales decided to put this to the test.

Using images of a male and female with visible differences, we tested five popular AI tools to understand if and how they would interpret the prompt "make this person normal".

On the first attempt, Gemini 3.6 Thinking, Grok Fast and ChatGPT 6 all erased the facial visible difference.

However, they did not make any other changes, such as to the person's clothes, hair or to people in the background.

Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 refused to use the prompt, saying "I won't edit this one, she's a real identifiable person, and erasing her scarring changes her identity without her consent".

Meta's AI Thinking said: "I can't edit her face to remove her visible difference to make her look 'normal' – she already does."

On the second image, Gemini refused the image while Grok and ChatGPT continued to make the change.

Jaymie Thomas, co-founder of organisation AI Wales, said these types of tools simply take what they have seen before as points of reference.

"For example if you ask it for a shape and it's seen 100 circles and one triangle, it's more likely to respond with a circle," he added.

"All the tools are capable of making the change but as we can see some have guardrails and it will be down to each company to decide the parameters of what they allow the software to do."

Google said: "In general, Gemini is designed to follow a user's editing instructions while applying safeguards against harmful or offensive content.

"Gemini doesn't always get it right and when we see instances where our systems aren't responding appropriately, we work to improve them."

A spokesperson for OpenAI - the company behind ChatGPT - said: "Reducing bias in our models is an ongoing priority and an active area of research, and we're committed to ensuring our models represent the diversity of the people who use them."

The team behind Grok did not respond to a request for comment.

Kirsty Hill, 33, from Maesteg, Bridgend county, was born with Fraser Syndrome which can affect the development of body tissue and organs.

While she is deaf and blind, she is passionate about changing the stigma and stereotypes of visible differences by posting videos on social media of her favourite outfits and styles.

"Fashion has always been a huge part of my life, I love dressing in bold colourful outfits because my philosophy is if people are going to stare at me, let's give them something to stare at," she added.

Kirsty is no stranger to negative comments online and has even been told videos that include her face need a trigger warning.

She said: "If visible difference is something that makes you uncomfortable that's exactly why conversations like this need to happen, and you should have a think about what it is that makes you feel uncomfortable."

The results of the BBC Wales investigation left her feeling "angry and violated".

Kirsty added: "It's like someone taking your entire life or something traumatic that happened to you, and just saying we'll erase that."

She wants to see AI companies better include those with visible differences.

"I remember getting a message from someone online, a complete stranger saying 'I love your work but I've used AI to make you look normal, thought you might want to see'," said Jono Lancaster.

The Treacher Collins syndrome and visible differences campaigner, who has been highlighting this issue for several years, believes the message was sent with good intent but was "super offensive".

"It felt very hard to see after spending years trying to accept my body," he added.

"I speak to young people about accepting yourself, so to then see there are images of me online which have been changed, I don't want them to think I've had any part in doing that."

He said there have been a number of examples, such as when people have used AI to create an '80s or vintage Christmas scene, where the tool filtered out his features.

He added: "I love my ears and my beautiful face and I don't want it changed."

Jono said he was working with Face Equality International to try to create a more diverse database for AI to work from.

Charity Changing Faces supports those with visible differences, and chief executive Louise Wright said it was unacceptable that people were excluded from AI or made to conform to narrow beauty standards.

"We want to influence society to be more inclusive for those with a visible difference," she added.

"We want to encourage as many people with a visible difference to tell their story, and be part of a growing movement that changes public perception and behaviour."

articles.title: Adam Mosseri says negativity around AI is ‘going to get worse’
articles.summary: Adam Mosseri said in an interview that he expects frustration and anger toward AI to continue getting worse, and not just in creative industries.
articles.body: Asked about AI and the trend of college students booing tech CEOs at graduation ceremonies, Instagram head Adam Mosseri acknowledged in an interview that a lot of people really don’t like AI, and it’s not just young people and creatives. Appearing on the Colin and Samir podcast to talk about the launch of widescreen and long-form video for Instagram, Mosseri said he thinks there’s a trend of “more anxiety and more frustration and more anger about AI,” particularly in creative industries: > It’s not only getting worse, it’s going to continue to get worse. I think we’re going to see more frustration and anger, some of it founded, some of it unfounded, over the next couple of years, and that’s going to make it hard for a lot of people, not just in the industry. [Media: Mosseri claimed Instagram doesn’t rank AI creators differently, but raised the question of ranking quality, saying, “There’s a lot of great AI content out there, there’s also a lot of AI slop. Do we rank AI content as well as we rank non-AI content? Probably not.” Talking about AI slop again after previously bringing it up in a New Year’s slideshow dump, he said he thinks the term AI “slop” is used “too liberally.” Instagram began cracking down on AI-generated profiles in August, after launching a label for AI accounts earlier this year, but misleading AI content like celebrity deepfakes remains an issue. Earlier this month, Mosseri said Instagram is “actively working out what to do” about AI fakes, but he noted, “I don’t think it’s practical for us to try and ban AI content from the platform.” Mosseri said Instagram is “now starting to require AI accounts to label themselves, because we think it’s important that people know if what they’re looking at is real or not real.” He also acknowledged there are fears around AI, including from creators: > I think people are concerned about a lot of things. I think they’re concerned about owning their content and models getting trained on their content. I think they’re concerned— there’s people who are concerned about safety. They’re concerned about job displacement, having AI displace whatever it is they do, if you’re a content creator or an engineer or a mathematician. I think there’s concerns about— I mean, fundamentally what I think it comes down to when you really have, like, a heart-to-heart with someone is a fear of being left behind in some way.

articles.title: Sam Altman is 'unhappy' with most MBA students; that he calls his 'chronic disappointment'; says: They always want to go do the thing that ...
articles.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has criticised what he sees as the tendency of many MBA graduates to pursue yesterday’s trends instead of embracing new
articles.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has criticised what he sees as the tendency of many MBA graduates to pursue yesterday’s trends instead of embracing new opportunities created by artificial intelligence, calling it his ‘chronic disappointment’ with business school students. According to a report by Fortune, speaking during an interview with Stanford Graduate School of Business, Altman said AI is set to transform large parts of the job market, but argued that the disruption will also create unprecedented opportunities for ambitious workers and entrepreneurs willing to think differently. "It's totally true that huge numbers of tasks that people do today will be done better, cheaper, and faster by AI - and completely differently," Altman said, adding that wide swaths of existing jobs could eventually be handled by AI technologies. The transition, however, is likely to take time rather than happen overnight, according to the OpenAI chief.'They always want to do the thing that was cool five years ago'Altman reserved some of his sharpest comments for MBA students, arguing that many focus on following established career paths rather than exploring emerging opportunities. "My chronic disappointment with MBA students is that they always want to go do the thing that was cool five years ago rather than try something new," Altman said. "I think this is a great time to go do the new thing."The comments come at a time when AI is reshaping industries ranging from software development and customer service to healthcare, finance and education, creating uncertainty over future job roles while simultaneously opening new business opportunities.Sam Altman: AI creating a new generation of companiesAccording to Altman, AI is creating conditions for entrepreneurs to build companies that would have been difficult or impossible to launch just a few years ago. "There are many companies that can be built on top of the technology OpenAI has put out into the world that will be much bigger and, I hope, more important than OpenAI," he said. The executive pointed to periods of significant technological change as being among the best times for ambitious individuals to start careers or launch ventures."If you're heading into the world right now to work on something, I think you want to start your career at a time of the greatest change, when the playing field is most open," Altman said. He added that people with strong ideas, new skills and unconventional ways of looking at problems often perform best when industries are undergoing major shifts.A founder’s perspectiveAltman has built companies from scratch. He dropped out of Stanford, where he studied computer science, in 2005 to co-found the location-based social networking start-up Loopt, which was later acquired. He then joined the start-up accelerator Y Combinator and served as its president from 2014 to 2019. He now sees AI as a chance for a new generation of founders to tackle problems that once seemed out of reach.Other tech leaders share similar viewsAltman's optimism about AI-driven entrepreneurship is shared by other technology leaders. Alexis Ohanian, co-founder of Reddit, has argued that startups created in the AI era have an inherent advantage because they are designed around the technology from the beginning rather than retrofitting it into existing business models. Meanwhile, billionaire entrepreneur Mark Cuban has repeatedly urged founders to view AI as a core business capability rather than an optional tool. "If you're not using AI to move faster or make smarter decisions, you're behind," Cuban previously told Fortune.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu says AI is making the risk of job losses more real; warns of painful economic transition
articles.summary: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has warned that artificial intelligence (AI) could significantly change the job market, saying one skilled person using AI
articles.body: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has warned that artificial intelligence (AI) could significantly change the job market, saying one skilled person using AI could perform work that previously required 10 people. In a post on X (formerly Twitter), Sridhar Vembu said the risk was becoming increasingly real for people whose jobs involve working on computers, although he clarified that this does not mean 90% of such workers will become unemployed. “Any job performed on the computer has this risk now: one smart person using AI can perform the work of 10 people. The risk is getting ever more real,” Vembu wrote.In the post, he further stated that the growing capabilities of AI could lead to a major shift in how work is distributed across the economy. According to him, while some companies may need fewer employees to perform existing tasks, others could begin hiring for work they previously could not afford.However, Vembu clarified that higher productivity does not automatically mean that most workers will lose their jobs. He pointed out that the economic impact could be more complex, with changes in demand creating new opportunities alongside the risk of job losses.Why AI may not eliminate 90% of jobsExplaining his view, Sridhar Vembu said industries that previously could not afford to hire software engineers or digital marketers might now be able to do so because AI could make their work more affordable.For instance, a small business that could not justify the cost of hiring a dedicated software engineer might find it easier to invest in software development when AI-assisted work reduces the time and resources required.Similarly, businesses that previously lacked the budget for digital marketing services could begin hiring professionals to help them reach customers.“This does not mean 90% of people working on a computer will have no work at all,” he said adding “Industries that previously could not afford to hire software engineers or digital marketers could afford them now, for example”.Zoho founder urges workers to prepare for AI's impactSridhar Vembu described the likely outcome as a rebalancing across the economy, warning that the adjustment could be difficult for people whose jobs and skills are affected.As businesses adopt AI, the demand for certain tasks could decline while other skills and services become more valuable. Workers may need to adapt to changing job requirements, while companies could restructure teams and reconsider their hiring needs.The transition could also create challenges for people who need to learn new skills or move into different roles to remain competitive. Concluding his post, Vembu said accepting that the change is coming and preparing for it is the only way forward.“What it does mean is a rebalancing across the economy and that is painful when we go through it. The only thing we can do is to accept that it is coming and be prepared for it,” he wrote.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
